# Horse warfare (chariot, cavalry, horse archers) (`cavalry_chariot`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by stirrup_saddle, spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage, selective_breeding
- Core idea: The horse gives speed for scouting, raiding, pursuit and a shock or missile strike on a flank. The light two-wheeled chariot with spoked wheels came first as a mobile platform for an archer; once horses were bred larger and men learned to ride and shoot, cavalry replaced it because a rider needs no vehicle, no level ground and half the horses. Horse archers who refuse close combat can destroy heavy infantry in open country (Carrhae, 53 BC), but cavalry cannot break steady infantry frontally and cannot take walls.
- Pitfalls:
  - The stirrup is not needed for shock cavalry; Macedonian, Parthian and Roman horsemen charged with lances from treed or horned saddles without it
  - The claim that the stirrup caused feudalism (Lynn White, 1962) is rejected by most historians
  - Horses will not ride into a solid line of men with spears; charges succeed when the infantry flinches first
  - A horse eats about 10 kg of fodder a day, so cavalry armies are tied to grass and season
  - Scythed chariots were a spectacular failure against disciplined troops
- History: global: c. 2000 BC – early spoked-wheel chariot burials on the Eurasian steppe (Sintashta, southern Urals); mesopotamia: c. 1800–1600 BC – chariot warfare in the Near East; 9th c. BC – Assyrian cavalry; egypt: c. 1650–1550 BC – chariot arrives with the Hyksos; 1274 BC – Kadesh, a major chariot battle described in Egyptian royal inscriptions; india: c. 1500 BC onwards – chariots in the Rigveda; war elephants and cavalry by the 4th c. BC; china: c. 1200 BC – chariots at Anyang (Shang); 307 BC – King Wuling of Zhao adopts mounted archery and nomad dress; greece: 4th c. BC – Macedonian Companion cavalry as the decisive arm of Philip II and Alexander; rome: 1st c. BC – legions rely on Gallic, German and Numidian allied cavalry; 53 BC – Crassus destroyed by Parthian horse archers at Carrhae; americas: 1493 – Spanish expedition brings horses to Hispaniola; 1519 – Cortés brings horses to Mexico; 17th–18th c. – Plains peoples become horse nations; africa: from c. 14th c. – cavalry states of the Sahel (Mali, Songhai, Bornu)
- Read:
  - David W. Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007)
  - Robert Drews, Early Riders: The Beginnings of Mounted Warfare in Asia and Europe (2004)
  - Xenophon, On Horsemanship (c. 355 BC)
